This system combines user-submitted annotations with automated analysis to create a collaborative platform where individuals can contribute and benefit from others' experiences. The system automatically identifies document structure and enables users to contribute detailed annotations about document layout and content. Through this collaborative platform, users can explore, share, and contribute to a growing collection of accessible document paths, allowing for a more inclusive experience.

While BERT has greatly enhanced NLP applications, its pre-training method still has limitations in considering the entire context and encoding varying levels of importance in words. XLNet addresses these issues by employing autoregressive language modeling, allowing it to handle the full context and handle word importance effectively. However, XLNet's pre-training method makes it difficult to create a single model representation, which we resolve by re-creating the encoder-based unidirectional modeling of BERT. Our work also introduces external regularization to improve the model's consistency, continuity, and reduce its risk of overfitting, leading to better performance across multiple NLP tasks, including language tasks, document classification, and question answering.

We conducted a study to evaluate the influence of stellar activity on TRAPPIST-1's observed features during transit spectroscopy, focusing particularly on its activity-related markers, such as Ca II H&K, H$\alpha$, and UV. Using synthetic starspots and addressing stellar activity data, we found that its radius and temperature can significantly affect the detection of various molecular features. For instance, detecting the CO feature in TRAPPIST-1 is feasible, but the influence of surface spots on detecting H$_2$O is limited, as long as spot coverage remains under 1.5% in the atmosphere. However, larger spots could mimic absorption features in multiple wavelengths, rendering its identification difficult. Additionally, our research indicates that monitoring Ca II H&K, H$\alpha$, and UV indices can help identify surface spots, although variations in their correlations suggest the need to monitor multiple wavelengths to accurately assess stellar coverage. For TRAPPIST-1, we found that its detectable spots would have minimal influence on planetary feature detection, as the index-derived coverage is consistently higher than actual spot coverage.

We will explicitly construct conformal metrics with constant curvature on Riemann surfaces featuring singularities using meromorphic data, and also create explicit conformal metrics with constant curvature on orbifolds from first principles. Building on this foundation, we formulate and establish Poincaré-Lefschetz type theorems for surfaces with singularities and closed 3-manifolds that have underlying structures of pluri-contact, contact, or Cauchy-Riemann, without imposing any specific constraints on their topological composition. A novel theoretical framework for the Lefschetz set of a transformation is also introduced, particularly for the cases where the transformation is loxodromic.

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface has been conducted. Although the centipede can fly, its primary method of moving at the air-water interface involves using its legs to swim. Video analysis was performed to analyze its swimming motion, which showed that the centipede uses its legs to create forces that propel it forward. The pattern of the legs alternates in time, but the pattern of the waves in the water interface follows the centipede's body. The force that moves the centipede forward comes from the difference in the water's pull on the waves in front of and behind the centipede's body. The frequency of the waves in the water's interface was measured, which was around 10.5 Hz. The findings suggest that the centipede's body movement drives the swimming motion, which is similar to the way other animals use waves to move through water.

The integration of the finite volume discontinuous Galerkin method with the finite difference time domain scheme has proven effective in accurately simulating the nonlinear shallow water equations. A specially adapted time-marching algorithm was utilized to incorporate the ground displacement field into the system's initial state. A coupled approach was utilized, combining the open-source codes Mflood and ADT to solve for both 2D/3D tsunami propagation and seafloor deformation. The latter module was integrated within Mflood to assess how small-scale submarine features influence tsunami propagation. A comparison with widely accepted analytical solutions and established numerical models validated the accuracy of the proposed method. Additionally, historical events, including the 1962 Valdivia earthquake lake displacement and the 2011 Tohoku earthquake lake deformation, were simulated and the results were analyzed. The retrieved water levels and wave periods showed good agreement with existing data and highlighted the presence of short wavelength phenomena and higher harmonics in the generated tsunamis.

Recent research suggests that the cosmic star formation rate density at z>6 is significantly lower than expected, leading to the discovery of a new class of rare, faint galaxies that emit X-rays but are undetectable in Hubble band images. These galaxies have been observed to have high star formation rates, high dust content, and high sub-millimeter luminosity, but their exact nature is still unclear. We conducted a study of two of these galaxies, z=6.97 and z=7.04, using the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array and found that their sub-millimeter and carbon monoxide line luminosity are comparable to other high-redshift galaxies. We found that their spectral indices and dust temperature are consistent with other high-z galaxies, but their low Hubble band luminosity suggests that they have very little stellar mass. We found that their low [CII]/[OI] ratio and high [NII]/[SII] ratio indicate that they have significant ionization from their own starlight. We found that their high gas mass and low Hubble band luminosity suggest that they have high metallicity, contrary to expectations for early galaxies. We found that their low Hubble band luminosity and high gas mass are consistent with the idea that they are immature systems that have not yet formed stars at a high rate.

We investigate the characteristics of static spherically-symmetric black holes within a seven-dimensional gravity framework modified by two additional topological terms. The structure of these modified Einstein equations yields an exact solution, enabling us to investigate the stability of these black holes under the influence of external scalar fields. The analysis reveals the presence of both stable and unstable black holes in this gravity environment.

In a long and narrow two-dimensional channel, we examine whether random packings of disks reach a stable condition. The disk packings are created using a method that gradually adds density, and their stability is evaluated through two sets of simulations. The simulations show that these stable packings have specific density and size characteristics, which are largely determined by the size of the disks, but not by the strength of the forces involved. Additionally, we observe that these stable packings have key features that arise from being packed in the channel.

Our research suggests that significant regional differences exist in how El Ni\~no events influence seasonal precipitation patterns across the globe. We examined how two PNINO events, which occur in distinct eastern Pacific and central Pacific regions, relate to changes in the dipole mode of precipitation. We found that PNINO events, whether eastern Pacific or central Pacific, significantly alter the usual precipitation patterns, leading to substantial regional differences, which differ substantially from the overall global average. These differences suggest that regional models, specifically designed to account for local climate dynamics, may significantly improve our ability to accurately predict and account for climate variability in the face of PNINO events.

When materials that don't have a regular structure are subjected to force, the way they're compressed isn't always uniform, but this can be minimized in a well-organized, granular substance called hexatic matter. Our experiments involved examining a mixture of plastic beads in a well-defined area and found that their internal movements match up perfectly when the matter is arranged in a specific, orderly pattern. As a result, any non-uniform movements don't affect their overall response to force. However, once this pattern is disrupted, their internal movements no longer match up, and one level of order starts to reduce the impact, particularly in substances made of spherical particles, but a different type of particle can start to increase the impact instead.

This research investigates a population model that incorporates various species interacting with a contaminated habitat containing a constant concentration of a toxin, which may be an invasive species in this context. The model considers the population of adults and a separate class representing newborns. To realistsically model the interaction between these groups, the study introduces a psychological effect that influences the rate at which adult organisms come into contact with the toxin. To analyze the model's dynamics, the authors initially investigate a singular perturbation, where a parameter representing a specific process is set to zero. They establish the existence and uniqueness of positive periodic solutions for the resulting reduced model and identify a limit system that is one dimension lower. Furthermore, the study identifies a manifold that is invariant under the dynamics, which contains all positive periodic solutions of the reduced model, thereby enabling the researchers to understand the dynamics of the original model in terms of a reduced set of variables.

The decidability of the full Lambek logic with both weakening and contraction is proven to be no harder than a specific full Lambek variant, which leads to novel proofs of two key outcomes: the decidability of this logic and the independence of contraction from all valid arguments.

Hierarchical taxonomies, such as those categorizing animals or computer file directories, organize items into a hierarchical structure.  However, learning  a  meaningful  representation  for  these  complex  hierarchies  within  a  Euclidean  spatial  framework  proves  difficult,  as  they  fail  to  accurately  capture  the  underlying  relationships.  In this paper, we  show  that  by  instead  representing  hierarchies  within  a  different  geometric  framework,  we  can  obtain  more  accurate  representations.  In  fact, we  demonstrate  that  by  projecting  hierarchical  structures  into  a  non-Euclidean  space,  we  can  obtain a representation that closely mirrors the inherent structure of the hierarchy itself.  In addition, we find that by utilizing the  geometric properties of  a  different  framework,  we  can achieve better results when classifying objects and perform more effective information extraction tasks compared to using traditional techniques designed for  Euclidean spaces.

A comprehensive approach to a one-particle model of the dipole moment operator is built upon the framework of the coupled cluster singles and doubles method. This framework relies on a high-order approximation of the dipole moment operator and incorporates the cluster operator into the approach. Our proposed approach effectively captures large interaction dipole moments when molecules interact along their main axes, particularly for hydrogen-bonding systems. Furthermore, by combining this approach with the coupled cluster singles and doubles method, we achieve accurate binding energies and electric properties for important hydrogen-bonding complexes. Notably, the dipole moment and quadrupole moment in this approach are derived analytically, and the associated response equations are linear in the perturbation, which contributes to the efficiency of the method. Notably, the approach does not rely on any empirical corrections when binding energies are calculated.

The sector of industrial decision making is in a state of industrial revolution 4.0, where the existing systems and the impact of external factors like uncertain energy supply and industrial growth on this sector, as well as the effect of COVID-19 and an uncertain energy price on consignment delays and budget inaccuracies, prompted the creation of a new decision making model. This model incorporates an interval type-2 fuzzy logic to handle the uncertainties that arise, as the existing type-1 models can not effectively handle the uncertainties that arise due to the unpredictable changes in the variables. This model includes a novel approach to the calculation of the distance between the variables, as well as a weighted approach to the aggregation of the variables, as these are the key components that enable the effective handling of the uncertainties that arise. This decision making model is further validated through the analysis of the existing data and the comparison of the existing systems and the new model and the results show that the new model is more efficient than the existing systems and the existing type-1 models. This is because the new model is based on a non-deterministic approach to the calculation of the distance between the variables, as this is the key component that enables the effective handling of the uncertainties that arise. This is further validated through the analysis of the existing type-2 and type-1 models and the results show that the new model is more efficient than the existing systems and the existing type-1 models. Cyber-Physical Systems, widely used in various applications, necessitate robust resilience in their operation. To ensure this, a cyber component must be capable of responding to potential physical failures. Traditionally, this involves pre-defined, automatic corrective actions. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of these responses is contingent on predetermined knowledge of attacks and consequences. To bridge this gap, this research proposes a novel, reinforcement learning-based approach for resiliency in CPS. To test this approach, a real-world case study was conducted on a quadcopter system, and the results demonstrate its superiority over pre-scripted control methods.

One of the most pressing issues in modern physics is the identification of a suitable dark matter particle. Axion-like particles and Massive neutrinos are among the leading candidates. This study explores the possibility that a particular form of dark matter, consisting of dark matter with approximate dark matter-like particles, may account for the observed dark matter density. Furthermore, we have placed significant constraints on the parameter space where axions with a mass of around 10 to the power of negative 21 electron volts can exist, based on data from cosmic microwave background radiation, large scale structure, and galaxy rotation curves. Our findings suggest that a particular range of parameters is excluded, including masses between 21 and 31 to the power of negative 21 electron volts and mixing angles between 0.01 and 0.1.

Consider a complete, non-compact Riemannian manifold M with dimension n greater than one, exhibiting complete scalar negative curvature. We derive a criterion for the existence of non-trivial harmonic functions on M, contingent on the growth rate of the Laplacian of the ground state of the corresponding Laplace-Beltrami operator L associated with the manifold. Specifically, the criterion hinges on the asymptotic behavior, as r approaches infinity, where r denotes radius, and the Laplacian grows at a rate of r to the power of alpha, with alpha greater than or equal to n-1 over 2 in these instances. Furthermore, this result necessitates no curvature assumptions beyond the scalar curvature of the manifold. Building on this, the criteria can be reevaluated in the context of manifolds with Ricci curvature bounds, resulting in the following: the criteria can be relaxed to include the scenario where the complete Riemannian manifold M has a higher curvature bound, i.e., a lower Ricci curvature.

Radio sources were used to study the polarization properties of the cosmic microwave background radiation by analyzing their polarization contributions. A large sample of nearby radio sources was analyzed to determine polarization characteristics. The results showed polarization levels decreasing with larger source sizes, indicating higher polarization for smaller sources. Medium-sized sources exhibited polarization levels lower than those of point sources. The findings were used to establish practical polarization contamination limits for the CMB, with values ranging from 0.001 to 0.01 percent for various angular scales.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical framework, based on matrices, that are frequently used in applications involving time series data. HMMs are designed to make inferences about unobservable underlying states, referred to as latent states, from observable data. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, HMMs are formulated using matrix-valued functions. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, HMMs are designed using continuous-valued matrices. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, HMMs are designed using optimization techniques, such as the type-I and type-II optimization problems. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, HMMs are designed using testing procedures, such as the testing of independence in HMMs. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, HMMs are designed using statistical tools, such as the estimation of transition probabilities, dynamic correlation, and spectral analysis. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, HMMs are designed using tools for testing model adequacy, such as the testing of independence in residuals and checking for time-variability in HMMs. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, HMMs are designed using tools for identifying and correcting model inadequacies in HMMs. In scenarios that involve continuous, rather than categorical, latent states, H

We develop a class of stochastic advection problems to investigate turbulent transport in transport equations driven by irrotational potential flows. The underlying turbulent flow is modeled as a stochastic process with space-dependent velocities and intermittent scalar fields. By utilizing probabilistic techniques, the study derives a probabilistic estimate of turbulence and demonstrates the existence of a probabilistic energy flux in the context of these equations. The outcome suggests that turbulent transport can be effectively studied through stochastic differential equations.

A novel method for assessing nuclear elastic scattering Frenkel folding models is to separately evaluate nuclear and Coulomb potentials, thereby eliminating uncertainties in their individual parameters. By utilizing experimentally obtained matter radii and depth ratios, the total potential can be effectively constrained. This has been successfully demonstrated using a series of elastic scattering experiments involving various medium-heavy nuclei and two distinct sets of Fresnel approximations, yielding satisfactory results. Notably, the chosen potential is well-suited for a broad range of systems and can be employed in place of various other folding potentials.

A comprehensive study of electromagnetic radiation interaction in a thin slab reveals novel thermodynamic properties. The work builds on cavity quantum electrodynamics in the high-temperature regime, where the radiation behaves as an ideal gas. In contrast, when the temperature is lowered, the slab's properties disrupt this analogy. This change is attributed to the emergence of non-linearities within the dipole model. Our analysis includes specific calculations for thermal expansion coefficients and osmotic pressure, demonstrating that these properties exhibit non-ideal behavior comparable to the interaction pressures of condensed matter systems. This may potentially enable the creation of condensed matter-like mimics using the slab setup.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements and multiple locations revealed within a short timeframe is an extremely difficult task. Existing approaches often struggle to safeguard against sophisticated attackers, such as those capable of cross-referencing locations with known information. In this paper, we introduce a new algorithm that uses an extended version of the Rubik's cube to protect user privacy while revealing their locations at different times. Our algorithm simulates cube transformations to confuse the attacker while sending the actual locations to the user. When locations are released in sequence, our algorithm ensures their apparent movement aligns with actual transformations, effectively safeguarding sensitive inter-location relationships.

Autonomous driving relies heavily on place recognition (PLARECOG) to navigate unfamiliar and unfamiliar settings, particularly when GPS signals are weak or absent. To address this, researchers have been using point cloud data for PLARECOG, as it is more consistent and detailed than RGB images. However, processing this data is computationally expensive, hindering real-time processing. A recent study proposes an efficient solution, combining and data augmenting point clouds before downscaling and utilizing a pre-trained ResNet20 to extract features, leading to improved performance. The solution outperformed existing methods, achieving an accuracy of 71.7% while maintaining an IoU of 54.8%, thanks to its faster processing speed.

Research on comparing groups using resting-state functional MRI is gaining traction, 
despite the challenges posed by individual differences in brain structure and function. 
To address these differences, complex statistical models have been developed, 
which enable researchers to draw conclusions from data collected across multiple sites. 
We have conducted an extensive review of the potential biases inherent in mult-site 
resting-state fMRI studies and the impact of these biases on study outcomes. 
To address these challenges, our research involved rigorous testing of two popular 
covariate adjustment methods in control datasets, which we also extended to mult-site 
resting-state fMRI data. 
Our findings demonstrate that multisite data significantly increases the likelihood of 
detecting substantial group differences, but this conclusion is contingent upon the 
inclusion of site variables in the analysis. 
Our results further indicate that both group homogeneity assessment and covariate 
adjustment strategies contribute to reducing statistical errors, 
which we believe can assist researchers in navigating the challenges posed by resting-state 
fMRI studies.

In a single-hop beeping network, stations interact via one-bit messages to exchange information and reach consensus. This study focuses on two problems: naming all stations and calculating the total number of stations, proposing two algorithms that achieve this with optimal efficiency, as no prior solutions had a runtime below O(n^(2/3)) stations. We provide a technique to develop beeping algorithms for these problems by adapting known non-beeping algorithms. The approach is demonstrated with an implementation for generating random permutations.

Code-mixing is a common language phenomenon where words, grammar, and sentence structure from one language blend with elements of another language, typically English. Creating code-mixed word embeddings is difficult due to the absence of high-quality language models and limited language pairs. This research introduces a framework, called Multilingual Code-Mix Embeddings (MoME), that enables the creation of code-mixed word embeddings. The framework incorporates one-to-one and many-to-one mapping, and uses this to train a neural network that produces code-mixed word embeddings. The MoME system can be extended to multiple source languages and was evaluated on three different mixing languages: Hindustani, Hindi-English and Marathi-English.

Using a combination of high-throughput density functional theory calculations and the linearized Eliashberg equations, we analyzed how the critical temperature of H3S responds to pressure, while also incorporating the influence of electron-phonon coupling and the energy range of interactions near the Fermi level. Our study reveals that the H3S phase delta function model overestifies the critical temperature at high pressures, with an estimated 2GPa threshold where a non-energy-independent model ceases to accurately describe the phase transition temperature.

This paper presents an innovative solution to motion planning challenges in dynamic environments where mobile robots rely on map-based and real-time data. The conventional method of integrating these data sources through time-consistent maps can be inefficient and is ineffective in fully understanding three-dimensional environments. To address the limitations of existing methods, we developed an alternative approach that employs predictive models and prioritizes outcomes rather than time consistency. The proposed method utilizes simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) algorithms to generate a two-dimensional map and a 3D point cloud, which is then used to predict and represent the environment in a probabilistic map and an occupancy grid, respectively. The probabilistic estimates are used to identify multiple feasible paths and the most suitable one is selected based on specific criteria. The proposed algorithm successfully incorporates map updates and is verified through simulation experiments involving an autonomous robot navigating an office environment.

This research presents a novel 3D surfel map for reliable self-localization in 
visual tasks, utilizing an efficient, adaptable, and conventional neural network 
to achieve accurate image matching. The proposed method, called progressive 
learning-based optimization of adaptive surfel maps, initially creates a detailed 
point cloud through visual odometry, and then develops an efficient surfel map. 
The method continuously refines the surfel reorganization using the least-surfel 
and adaptive updates, and then trains a compact model to achieve accurate 
image matching. The method demonstrates superior performance in adaptive 3D 
maps, and progressive learning-based self-localization compared to current 
techniques.

Reconstructing an $N$-dimensional group-sparse signal from $M$ underdetermined equations is explored, where the group sparsity leads to sparse group lasso solutions. A new group-sparse Lasso optimization algorithm is proposed based on accelerated primal-dual methods. The proposed approach offers improved reconstruction quality and reduced computational complexity. Theoretical analysis confirms the convergence rate of $O(1/t)$ for the sequence of iterates and a linear convergence rate after a sufficient number of iterations. The performance of the proposed approach is validated in simulation, which demonstrates its efficiency and superior performance in comparison to the existing proximal gradient algorithm.

We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve has a finite set of generators over a specific semifield. This involves identifying a particular finite set that generates the semifield. Furthermore, for the case of a plane tropical curve, we provide a concrete bound on the degree of a rational function to have a generating set over that semifield. Our results also extend to a non-archimedean field by establishing a relationship between a rational function's zeros and poles on a tropical curve and a certain polytope formed by power series coefficients.

This note primarily focuses on deriving a quasi-stationary distribution for the three-dimensional Brownian motion within a bounded domain that has smooth boundaries and satisfies the non-tangent sphere condition, under the influence of a killing mechanism. Additionally, the note also explores the connection between quasi-stationary distributions and eigenfunctions of the Dirichlet Laplacian. Additionally, we provide an explanation for why under spherical symmetry, the quasi-stationary distribution converges to the normalized density of the exit time rather than the eigenfunction corresponding to the first non-zero eigenvalue.

We demonstrate that under the condition that G is a simple group, there exists an infinite set of ankhedron diagrams, which are complete up to a certain equivalence relationship within G, and these can be expressed as products of specific graphical invariants known as Vassiliev invariants. Each of these graphical invariants has a specific order that is strictly less than the order of the given group, G.

The connection between unconventional superconductivity and antiferromagnetism has been an ongoing mystery in physics due to conflicting reports. The iron-based superconductor LiFeAs exhibits this connection in a unique way and displays Hall resistivity that deviates significantly from expectations near the critical temperature of superconductivity. The unusual behavior of Hall resistivity is attributed to a drastic change in carrier density that cannot be explained by conventional superconductivity theories. The carrier density in LiFeAs is found to be comparable to that of a ferromagnetic metal and not significantly affected by antiferromagnetic order. The unusual properties of LiFeAs suggest the presence of a new type of superconducting state where the two types of electrons are coupled in a way that is different from conventional superconductors.

Future measurements of light Higgs boson properties and the proposed lepton collider mission will significantly enhance our understanding of Type-II two Higgs doublet models. The improved constraints will notably reduce the model's viable parameter space, particularly in terms of the loop-induced processes $h\hbox{}_{125}Z~\gamma$, $h\hbox{}_{125}ZZ$, and $h\hbox{}{}_{125}\gamma$. The sensitivity to deviating Higgs boson couplings will also tighten bounds on the mass splitting between H and A, as well as set a lower mass limit for the H, assuming the absence of H and A detections at the Large Hadron Collider.

We demonstrate through simulation that neuroevolutionary learning can automatically design particles that assemble themselves into complex structures without any pre-existing knowledge. Using a combination of evolution algorithms and neural network-based control, we successfully create a variety of particles that form specific geometries upon applying electromagnetic fields, including tetrahedrons and octahedrons. Notably, our approach requires no prior assumptions about the physical mechanisms involved in the self-assembly process, allowing it to be applied to various systems that exhibit similar characteristics.

We're examining chiral gauge theories, specifically $SU(N)$ gauge theories with $N_f$ flavors of Dirac fermions, to understand their behavior. These theories can be divided into two distinct phases: the dynamical-Higgs-phase, where fermions break the gauge symmetry, and the Coulomb-phase. Our focus is on the dynamical-Higgs-phase, which can be broken down into two further phases. These new phases, separated by a first-order phase transition, can be characterized by the presence of local operators with non-zero expectation values. One phase is characterized by operators with $\Delta_{op} > N_f - 2N$, while the other is characterized by operators with $0 < \Delta_{op} < N_f - 2N$. We've also investigated the stability of these phases, which can be affected by quantum fluctuations, and found that one phase is stable while the other is unstable.

This study contributes to finite-dimensional approximation methods for stationary solutions of Navier-Stokes equations in cases where existence and uniqueness are still uncertain in non-three-dimensional cases. We investigate the approximation of smooth stationary solutions by spectrally truncated stationary Navier-Stokes equations, proving convergence for non-three-dimensional and non-smooth high energy solutions in certain $L_q$ spaces. This analysis shows that the truncated equations have a unique solution, implying that high-energy behavior of stationary Navier-Stokes equations can be understood through its truncated counterpart.

We are exploring the influence of nonlinear magnon-magnon interactions on a specific type of collinear insulator magnet that has a spiral magnetic structure. Our analysis shows that as magnons with different wave vectors interact, their polarization significantly changes. The higher-order interactions also result in noticeable energy shifts within the different branches of the magnon spectrum. The magnitude of the expected polarization modification depends on the specific type of crystal structure in the material and the temperature at which the measurement is taken. The findings suggest that dynamic light scattering measurements could be used to detect these polarization changes in a range of collinear magnetic insulators that have an orthorhombic structure, such as HoBO3 and ErGaO3.

A proposed modification for the originally secure Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem is analyzed, which has $2^{\geq 114}$ possible key recovery attacks. To increase the system's resistance, random permutations of a higher dimension are employed and a second modification involves using a different type of linear code, specifically dual-type, in the public key instead of Reed-Solomon codes.

To improve pre-trained language models, which can represent any sentence's meaning from its beginning to the end, we need to ensure consistent representations. Our approach, UniRep, introduces a novel type of pre-trained language model that learns a unified representation for any sentence in raw text. By utilizing this model, UniRep can be used to train multiple pre-trained tasks simultaneously, such as part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and others. Furthermore, UniRep has been successfully applied to create tasks like sentence compression, which involves summarizing a long story into a shorter, informative version.

A novel minimum spanning acycle is introduced and its empirical weighting is shown to converge in the infinite vertex setting. This outcome can also be derived from the empirical weighting of a specific minimum spanning tree within a conditional framework related to the acycle. This tree is connected to a minimal spanning tree of a modified set of points, which is obtained by removing the acycle's edges. Furthermore, the acycle's total weighting is proven to conform to the 2D and 3rd dimension Brownian motion models, which were established by Hartley and Van Handel.

Federated learning is a decentralized machine learning paradigm, enabling the collaboration of multiple clients to train a global model without disclosing sensitive client data. In this framework, clients hold various attributes of individuals, such as age and income. There are two primary federated learning paradigms: horizontal, where multiple clients possess overlapping client sets but different local models, and vertical, where a single client possesses disjoint client sets, each with a different local model, or cross-client inference. This paper explores the challenges of cross-client federated learning, particularly in vertical learning, and introduces two new protocols, FedPer-V and FedPer-V2, which generalize the FedPer learning framework to the vertical domain. These new protocols leverage PER's model perturbation technique to mitigate client data privacy issues without requiring a centralized server.

A new, intriguing process called baryogenesis through B mesons has been explored. B mesosynthesis, a theoretical framework that uses the dynamics of B mesons and baryons to create an initial asymmetry between matter and antimatter, has recently been found to be able to induce not only baryon asymmetry but also lepton asymmetry. However, a detailed examination of B mesogenesis via the processes involving the decay of B baryons into a lepton and a neutron or a antilepton and a proton has so far been limited. Research shows that these specific decays can indeed create both lepton and baryon asymmetries, with potential contributions from interference between different decay types and resonant effects. A detailed analysis of this phenomenon is conducted, focusing on how this mechanism generates asymmetries and how it compares to other established processes, such as the Standard Model's electroweak baryogenesis, under the conditions of inflation.

In a Smart City, interconnected smart devices and integrated systems enable
efficient problem-solving and optimization. To capitalize on the City's intelligence,
a collaborative framework is implemented, allowing various entities to work together.
However, Terrorists aim to disrupt these smart systems, posing a threat to public safety.
This study examines terrorist attacks on smart systems and their impact on the City.
A smart terrorist model is introduced, where a terrorist network collaborates to
maximize their impact while minimizing the risk of exposure and city resilience.
A Monte Carlo-based multi-objective optimization model is designed to predict
the consequences of terrorist attacks. The analysis reveals how various factors,
including weapon type, attack timing, and response time, affect the number of
casualties.

Researchers examined the properties of Reissner-Nordström black holes within an expanded space, considering specifically the scenarios where the phase transition temperature is lower than its critical point. They explored how these transitions are related to the dynamics of REISSNER-NORDSTRÖM black holes across a wide range of expansion pressures, analyzing specifically the scenarios where the critical point does not exist within this phase. Researchers further investigated the oscillation patterns of REISSNER-NORDSTRÖM black holes as they vary in size and speed, considering specifically the scenarios where the critical point does not exist within this expansion space. Researchers also explored specifically the scenarios where the critical point does exist within this expansion space, analyzing specifically the relationships between the critical points' existence and the patterns of redefined van der Waals transitions that black holes undergo.

Long document retrieval has become a growing concern in recent reading comprehension competitions. Recent solutions have shown promising results in tasks requiring long document understanding, yet they often overlook the challenges posed by noise and irrelevant information. To address this issue, we've developed LiHT, a new approach combining two key components. LiHT employs a contrastive learning method to develop robust representations that can effectively filter out noisy information, and it further enhances these using a self-supervised task that encourages the model to focus on crucial document sections. LiHT has been demonstrated to outperform recent top competitors on multiple challenges, showcasing better robustness and more effective section representation through the liHT's contrastive learning and self-supervised training methods.

As graph representation learning applications expand, self-supervised graph learning is gaining attention due to its unlabeled data efficiency. Recent pseudo-labeling methods, which utilize pre-trained GNNs to assign labels to unlabelled graph nodes, have been developed. Nevertheless, these approaches overlook the problem of label imbalance, which can lead to suboptimal pseudo-labels and hinder performance when incorporating pseudo-labels into the training process. To address this limitation, we propose a pioneering pseudo-labeling framework that prioritizes selecting high-quality, balanced labels. By pre-training a GNN using self-supervised learning and then refining it with pseudo-labels, our framework overcomes the disparity between offline and online pseudo-labeling methods. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple datasets.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an effective tool for analyzing the dynamics of injected electrons produced by plasma wakefield acceleration when driven by high-intensity laser pulses. The distinct spectral features of this radiation are influenced by electron injection conditions and can thus provide valuable insights into the process. Theoretical and numerical analysis shows that variations in the electron density profile and the column's geometry can be accurately determined by examining these spectral features. Furthermore, high-resolution spectral analysis allows researchers to distinguish between different injection mechanisms at play during the electron acceleration process.

This study introduces the first fully verified methods for privately learning decision trees in a hierarchical manner across a network of devices. The proposed algorithm, DP-TopDown, provides secure tree learning and presents two distributed variations: DP-TopDown-G and DP-TopDraw. DP-TopDraw is the initial secure, distributed learning algorithm to employ a private summing method across the network. The study experimentally evaluates the proposed algorithms using real-world data and demonstrates their effectiveness in accurately labeling data while maintaining high data utility and secure privacy.

We focus on the variational inference task of minimizing a R\'enyi divergence regularized with a constraint, particularly when the constraint is an entropy minimum. The problem of minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence under an entropy minimum is well-established in information geometry. However, the information-geometric connections for all values of the parameter $\alpha$ are yet to be fully explored. We introduce a novel geometric interpretation using two manifolds, the exponential manifold and the hyperbolic manifold, to describe the optimization process. The projection of the exponential manifold onto the hyperbolic manifold along a geodesic provides an intuitive understanding of the optimization process, revealing an iterative relationship between two fixed distributions.

This generalises the discrete Bayesian network class to the chain event graph class, allowing for unordered variables, anabelian modifications, and label changes. A GE model is defined by a directed graph with associated probability parameters, similar to a Bayesian network. We introduced a new method for Bayesian analysis in the chain event graph model and found that the most probable parameters have distinct estimates for every subgraph in the directed graph. Additionally, an information measure was introduced to analyse the difference between two GE models, based on a statistical measure that can also be used for Bayesian analysis.

In this research, a comprehensive study is presented for solving convex minimization
issues in a per-function model, utilizing the forward-backward and dual forward-backward
methods along with Tikhonov regularization to reach an $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ convergence rate.
A novel stochastic forward-backward algorithm, derived from a forward-backward scheme with
dual forward-backward and Tikhonov regularization, is proposed to satisfy a budget of
computations. This solution involves executing the novel algorithm $\tau$ times, performing
a dual forward-backward step, and solving a quadratic problem, all while maintaining
a strict stochastic constraint. This approach is applied to a wide range of problems
including multilinear regression, multilinear low-rank matrix completion, and multilinear
matrix factorization.

This study explores the effects of proximity to walls on agents with limited decision-making capabilities. Despite having no awareness of their surroundings, such agents show a remarkable ability to navigate around obstacles without getting stuck, often traversing walls and navigating around corners seamlessly. Notably, while the agents' individual behaviors are relatively straightforward, their collective movement patterns become increasingly complex as the path they follow adapts to the contours of the wall, effectively following its general direction. We introduce a new approach to understanding these phenomena by using the concept of a 'decision cone' to model how agents make choices, and through simulations, we identify characteristics of agents with minimal awareness that enable them to successfully navigate near walls.

Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, the effects of impurities on the transport properties in cuprate superconductors have been explored.  Focusing on hole-doped, YBCO, and FBCO superconductors with microwave frequency and temperature, our findings reveal an unusual pattern.  Microwave conductivity initially decreases with increasing temperature, only to increase again at higher temperatures.  This behavior is more pronounced in samples with lighter mass ratio $M_m = m^*/m^*_0$ and lower carrier concentration of impurities.  Interestingly, our results show that impurity scattering does not significantly impact the critical temperature.  However, it can affect the temperature dependence of the critical temperature near the superconducting transition temperature, under certain conditions.  This may offer a potential avenue for studying the superconducting mechanism in cuprates by introducing impurities.

This passage discusses an anisotropic curvature flow, referred to as a crystalline curvature flow, which is characterized by energy release in a specific manner, in contrast to isotropic counterparts. Notably, the passage focuses on an anisotropic curvature flow, known as an anisotropic mean curvature flow, and its more general forms. The analysis is primarily centered on short-time properties, encompassing existence, uniqueness, and regularity. Key aspects of the discussion include handling singularities like anisotropic cusps and singular points.

Plant growth is a complex process that responds to various internal and external stimuli, such as light, water, and nutrients. To maximize their survival, plants adapt their growth patterns based on these stimuli, often resulting in the development of specialized structures like tendrils in vines. Vine tendrils, in particular, respond to touch stimuli by coiling to support the plant's upward growth. This natural process can be harnessed to create adaptive structures in architecture and art by incorporating stimuli-responsive materials that mimic the behavior of vine tendrils. Such innovations can lead to the creation of responsive art pieces and the integration of intelligent structures into architecture, thereby enhancing human interaction with the built environment and fostering sustainable design.

It has been demonstrated that the SLE loop measure arises from the Liouville quantum gravity disk using conformal welding methods similar to those applied in the Schramm-Loewner-Kiforvi (LSK) model. Furthermore, this demonstration yields the recovery of specific structural properties similar to those found in the LSK model, specifically related to the evolution family and cluster structure of the Liouville quantum gravity explorers. Additionally, this demonstration provides an alternative perspective on the random surface results originally obtained by the Smith and Schramm-Loewner-Kiforvi model.

The Image Biomarker Standardisation Initiative is a global research project that is working towards standardizing and improving communication in the field of image biomarkers and machine learning applications within medical imaging. This project is focused on developing consistent methods to measure image-based characteristics and facilitating the evaluation of images' predictive capabilities.

We have examined the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on a specific process, specifically $\gamma p \to \pi^{0} p$ and $\gamma p \to K^{+} n$. Our results for these reactions show that considering these resonances significantly alters the presence of a distinct peak in a related process and as a result, aligns with experimental data. Furthermore, our analysis of kaon photoproduction yields results that generally agree with available experimental data when accounting for the influence of these resonances.
This research describes the process of pre-processing raw images to convert them into usable, semantically annotated data. The dataset and code used in the study will be made publicly accessible.

Building upon our previous research, we re-examined the constraints imposed by globular clusters on primordial black holes, which are also prime black hole dwarf spheroidal candidate components. These constraints were then used to evaluate the possibility of primordial black holes serving as dark matter, as well as dark matter within globular clusters. If primordial black holes constitute dark matter, their mass is confined to a specific range: $1.39 \times 10^{36} \ \rm kg \le M_{PBH} \le 1.67 \times 10^{38} \ \rm kg$. To prevent observational data from globular clusters from contradicting them, the fraction of primordial black holes contributing to dark matter cannot exceed approximately 10%.

University administrators are in a perpetual quest to optimize course scheduling and
resource allocation to best serve students. Several key variables influence student
course enrollment patterns, including individual academic and career aspirations,
course prerequisites, timing, cost, and course capacity. To effectively address these
issues, it is crucial to create robust decision support systems. To this end, researchers
have proposed an innovative approach to predicting student course demand, incorporating
user attributes, as well as the dynamic characteristics of course and departmental
subgraphs. The proposed system leverages a novel, multi-task learning framework that
allows the prediction of student course demand over time and across varying capacity levels.
To ensure the model's efficiency and scalability, it is optimized through a combination of
model compression techniques, including pruning and quantization. The proposed model
outperforms competing optimization models and machine learning algorithms, showcasing
its exceptional scalability in handling large university enrollment datasets.

This study examines the distance control methods used in connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) for platooning, focusing on the vehicle that follows the leader. CTV platoon spacing is achieved through two approaches: time-head way (TW) and distance head way (DH). This study's results show that DH and CTV methods often lead to out-of-bound vehicle velocities, whereas TW and CTV speeds tend to align with the speed limits, making them a more viable option.

One of the most extensively employed machine learning algorithms is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which involves iteratively estimating the gradient of the loss function based on randomly selected data subsets.  This algorithm can be adapted to large-scale distributed computing environments by dividing computations across multiple processes, which independently calculate gradients and exchange model information regularly during each iteration.  This distributed SGD approach can achieve linear scalability, which means it can reduce the processing time proportionally to the number of employed CPUs.  However, due to the frequent model exchanges required, the overall performance gain is often hindered by the overhead of communication.  This limitation can be overcome through the development of an efficient, communication-avoidance optimization technique called CA-SGD, which significantly reduces the frequency of model exchanges required, which in turn leads to considerable gains in execution time.  This technology has been implemented and tested across a range of datasets, demonstrating its potential to achieve up to 3.5x time speedup over traditional SGD methods in real-world applications.

The widespread dissemination of misinformation and misinformation disguised as news via social media has led to a significant issue. As a result, distinguishing between fake and real content has become a significant challenge. Humans struggle to identify the authenticity of content shared on social media, including news headlines. In this research, a novel approach is proposed to improve the capabilities of Transformer models in generating fake news detection by fine-tuning them on specific tasks such as title or summary generation, or by providing summaries along with titles. This approach has been tested on two datasets, the Facebook Page Sedition Dataset and the Facebook Title and Summary Sedition Dataset. It is observed that the suggested method yields better results on both datasets.

Future large-scale radio interferometers, intended for imaging the 21-cm signal throughout the Epoch of Reionization and the Epoch of Cosmological Reionization, may struggle with delays caused by traditional correlator architectures. These systems, typically based on real-time calculations, can limit the amount of data that can be processed due to the limited processing power of their digital circuits. As a result, there is a need for an alternative architecture that can efficiently process the data. One proposed solution is the FFT-correlator architecture, which scales more efficiently with the amount of data. However, the level of imaging quality can be compromised by the compromise in the frequency resolution used. This research investigates the feasibility and performance of using FFT-correlator architectures for future interferometers by comparing them to traditional correlators. The outcomes indicate that using an FFT-correlator architecture with reduced frequency resolution can still produce accurate results, potentially saving processing time and power requirements by a factor of up to 100 times for large data sets.

Predicting future financial time series based on historical data is a critical task for risk management and trading.  However, traditional methods such as conditional GANs can struggle with long-term dependencies, limiting their effectiveness.  To address this, we've developed conditional Variational Autoencodes (cVAE) as an alternative to conditional GANs for generating and forecasting financial time series data.  We've also developed a new model, the Logarithm VAE, which improves sampling quality and provides a closed-form sampling process.  Extensive testing on multiple stock market datasets has demonstrated that our models, particularly the Logarithm VAE, outperform other competing methods in generating and forecasting financial time series data.

We have derived the polarized massive operator matrix element $A_{gq}^{(3)}(N)$ to three-loop order in QCD and provide the general representation involving triple sums, along with further decomposition into single and double sums involving non-zero mass contributions. We also detail all relevant three-loop diagrams and their corresponding massive one-loop matrix elements, presenting explicit expressions for specific sum terms, such as diagonal elements, while outlining the method to derive off-diagonal elements. Furthermore, the result is implemented into QCD predictions and is demonstrated in the perturbative decay of the $Z$ boson into a quark-antiquark pair in the big-Bag experiment.

A notable achievement of the Fermi-LAT gamma-ray satellite has been the identification of numerous blazars in the MeV energy range. Researchers categorize these blazars into two types: FSRQs and BL Lacs, based on their characteristics. BL Lacs are particularly challenging to study because they are classified as 'featureless' due to the absence of an optical emission line and strong emission features. This study employs a novel deep learning approach using a ResNet neural network to analyze light curves of Fermi-LAT gamma-ray sources. The proposed framework combines spatial frequency domain filtering with a fully convolutional neural network, to extract valuable information from both spatial and temporal image features. This framework extracts features from two-dimensional images, which are then fed into the ResNet neural network for classification. The framework achieved an accuracy of 90.5% on 10-fold cross-validation, significantly outperforming previous results with an accuracy of 68.3%. Furthermore, binary cross-entropy and a two-step data augmentation process were applied to enhance classification performance. The analysis of feature maps generated by the ResNet revealed the two types of blazars, supporting their classification. This research also suggests that the Fermi-LAT catalog could potentially include more BL Lac objects, which are crucial for studying BL Lacs.

Active participation is essential for the growth of social networking platforms, which in turn requires engaging content for users to share with others. Recent advancements have led to the creation of various media formats for different forms of self-expression. However, existing algorithms for assigning users to groups are inadequate, as they only consider existing connections when deciding on new user associations. This paper introduces a novel association recommendation algorithm, which, despite challenging data limitations, successfully predicts users and groups that are likely to be associated. The proposed algorithm leverages various social and media features using lightGBM. The results of our study demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, while showing a significant correlation with users' group associations after joining a platform.

This paper introduces the concept of tensor join for hypergraphs, deriving its hypergraph homomorphism number formula and exploring properties using the tensor join. We find the formula for the hypergraph homomorphism number of the hypergraph path and tree join, in addition to analyzing several characteristics of the tensor join.

India's next space observatory, the INSIST, is a large space-based observatory designed to make significant contributions across the full range of its capabilities, from small to large apertures. This ambitious project, set to launch in the early 2030s, is a 1.2-meter space telescope equipped with two narrow-field and two wide-field cameras, and a spectrograph that can analyze up to 5000 objects at a time. With an innovative design, the INSIST will be a low-cost space mission that will serve multiple purposes, including the study of exoplanets, galaxies, and cosmic structures. This space observatory will play a crucial role in addressing the pressing challenges of the future, such as the need to combine ground-based and space-based observations, and to study the properties of both young and old galaxies. This document provides an overview of the INSIST's design, design choices, and its intended capabilities, and serves as an invitation for the scientific community to collaborate and contribute to this ambitious space mission.

In clinical trials, linear mixed model repeated measures is commonly employed for the primary analysis. However, treating categorical time as a continuous variable in this model may introduce bias when time-continuum assumptions are violated. Instead, highly flexible non-parametric methods such as cubic spline basis functions can be utilized to model time effects accurately without assuming a continuous variable. Although these methods offer a solution, they often come with a high number of parameters to estimate, making interpretation difficult. To balance this, we propose using Bayesian estimation of cubic spline models with hyperpriors on the spline coefficients, effectively acting as an automatic model selection among various spline models. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulation studies, showing that it performs well at different sample sizes compared to other Bayesian estimation methods. Finally, a real-world rheumatoid arthritis trial is presented to showcase the utility of Bayesian spline models.

A novel computational method called Action-based Flux Sampling (AFFlux) has been introduced to identify key components of reaction pathways, including transition paths, state spaces, and bottleneck connections. This method, rooted in non-equilibrium thermodynamics, utilizes the Onsager-Machlup action to quantify action flux across diverse reaction pathways in a given time frame. By employing A* search, the 'shortest' transition paths among molecular configurations can be identified through action distances, while calculating the minimum action through the graph involves dynamic programming. Our research validates the 'AUFFLUX' algorithm on the C60 fullerene, revealing its ability to identify critical components of complex reaction pathways under the influence of thermal fluctuations. This discovery highlights the action's maximum capacity to identify the most significant components of reaction pathways, which cannot be achieved by simply examining entropy and energy distributions.

This study focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE-based method akin to Phong et al to derive and establish L-infinity and Holder estimates across all scales. These results encompass a parallel progression towards a continuous analog of the Monge-Ampere flow in the context of gradient flow.

Building on the idea of measure and phase from transducers, we extend this concept to a broader class of automata that operate over arbitrary, potentially infinite monoids. We discover that this generalized class, comprising polyregular functions, includes all previously recognized specialized classes of transducers. We establish a complete framework for analyzing the complexity of these specialized classes by identifying a complete set of complexity metrics. Furthermore, we create theoretical tools to analyze the asymptotic behavior of sequences and sets of strings processed by the automata, as well as two theorets that facilitate decomposition of complex sequences and strings. We apply these tools to derive precise complexity functions for the most significant instances of these specialized classes of transducers.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the 'correction' term requiring consideration of Lions-type measure derivatives to determine necessary cross-correlations. It positions this framework in the context of SDEs influenced by conditional measure flows, with the solution being a adapted process. This approach enables SDEs to be integrated with respect to absolute continuous processes and measure flows, with special cases being explored, including SDEs driven by lattice random walks and their functional pathwise interpretation.

This study aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups within $N$-normal subgroups and introduces several novel concepts. A subgroup $H$ of a group $G$ is termed $N$-normal if the normalizer of $H$ in $G$ equals the center of $G$. We examine the properties of these subgroups and demonstrate that the intersection and product of $N$-normal subgroups are themselves $N$-normal. A subgroup $H$ is defined as primitive when it is both a normal subgroup of $G$ and its centralizer is contained within $H$ itself. A novel approach is proposed to identify primitive subgroups. A prime subgroup $P$ of group $G$ is termed almost $N$-normal if it possesses a normalizer that is $G$-normal, and such a subgroup is primitive if and only if it has a centralizer of $G$. We investigate a novel notion of a subgroup being a near-normalizer of another, and establish that if a normal subgroup of $G$ is a near-normalizer of another, it is almost $N$-normal. A unique prime subgroup of $G$ is termed a hyper-regular subgroup if its normalizer is an $N$-normal subgroup of $G$.
