This study addresses the challenge of generating SQL semantics from natural language across different domains, where domain adaptation and model robustness are of paramount importance. We introduce a simplified version of the multi-domain text to SQL parsing task called isolated-domain text to SQL parsing, where the model is assumed to be isolated within each domain and is not permitted to draw information from other domains. This is achieved through the development of a new dynamic isolation-aware adversarial parser (IAP) that not only optimizes the model's parsing performance within each domain but also identifies the significance of each input. The IAP employs an attention-based encoder to create a dynamic isolation map, which is then used by an adversarial dynamic graph neural network (ADGNN) to pinpoint domain-isolation-sensitive features. Furthermore, we propose a novel reward mechanism that incorporates graph robustness into the training process to further enhance model generalization. Comprehensive experiments on the Spider dataset have validated the superiority of our proposed IAT and our IAT-Reward, which outperforms the current best approaches and even excels in the full-domain multi-task setting.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating each robot amidst obstacles poses a significant challenge. Traditional approaches rely on omniscient knowledge, which is impractical in real-world scenarios. In contrast, inquiring sensors can gather spatial data on obstacles, aiding navigation. However, this approach introduces information asymmetry between the omniscient and inquiring sensor views. To address this, we develop a mechanism for view-inquiring based multi-robot navigation, where the inquiring sensor sees only a subset of obstacles, whereas the omniscient view captures the full spatial layout of obstacles. In this work, we formulate the view-inquiring problem as minimizing a specific metric, distributionally robust CVaR, of navigation costs. In doing so, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to balance the two views, ensuring a balance between vision quality and privacy. We prove the existence of a unique, optimal solution to this problem, and provide data-driven methods to find it. We also establish the convergence of these methods under certain conditions. In experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed solution.

Recent data from the Gaia mission has allowed researchers to investigate the outer halo of the Andromeda galaxy by examining its most distant, metal-poor satellite Andromeda XXV. Andromeda XXV is a dwarf galaxy that is roughly 1.2 million light-years away from our own galaxy and contains a sparse collection of stars. Researchers have been able to determine the galaxy's movement and physical location relative to the Andromeda galaxy by analyzing space movements of stars within the galaxy using precise data from Gaia. Andromeda XXV's movement suggests that it is likely on its first encounter with the Andromeda galaxy and is moving along a roughly circular path. Andromeda XXV's metal content is lower than what is typically found in other Local Group dwarf galaxies. Andromeda XXV's low luminosity suggests it is a very small galaxy. Andromeda XXV's movement and chemical composition are consistent with theories about galaxy formation.

In massive machine-type communications, utilizing grant-free access reduces latency and enhances efficiency, making it ideal for scenarios requiring urgent transmission of data with high packet success rates. However, concurrent transmissions from multiple devices increase the risk of signal overlap, leading to failed packets and compromising the communication process. To address this challenge, we present an innovative packet replication approach, where devices transmit the same data to several groups with higher failure rates, allowing for successful communication even when some devices fail to transmit. By optimizing these repetition rates, we develop an effective load control strategy that minimizes network congestion while ensuring a high packet success rate for urgent transmissions.

A standard approach to thermodynamics of moist air relies on combining equations of state for dry air and water vapor with interaction terms. Our approach utilizes various thermodynamic potentials to provide a more comprehensive framework for thermodynamic modeling of moist air. This framework can accommodate multiple equations of state and is more transparent in showing how different models are derived. A specific implementation of this methodology using the ideal gas law for dry air and a combination of ideal gas law and scaling correction for water is demonstrated.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. These new algebraic objects may be viewed as semirings and monoids within a more comprehensive structure of semirings and monoids, with a modified definition of identity. A specific relationship is defined that resembles ideal multiplication in multidegrees, applicable to ideals within these algebraic objects. When examples of algebraic objects, which are more complex than semirings and monoids but still retain useful properties, are identified, they demonstrate that ideal multiplication within these algebraic objects sometimes has more than one valid outcome.

Research on spoken dialogue systems has traditionally centered around a limited set of best ASR outputs, but this approach fails to capture the full range of possible outcomes and hampers the learning process. Confusion networks, which provide a more comprehensive and probabilistic view of data, have shown potential in the field but have largely been confined to the ASR community. This paper explores the benefits of using confusion networks in the planning stage of a spoken dialogue system, analyzing their representational potential and the feasibility of learning from them within a theoretical decision-making framework, specifically the Partially Observable Markov Decision Process. To framework this exploration, we proposed a new structure, the spoken dialogue Partly Observable confusion network decision process, which enables the analysis of both policy and value in the context of spoken dialogue systems. This paper also presents a probabilistic planning algorithm and an algorithm for multistep dynamic programming, which are novel contributions to the field. The research demonstrates that using confusion networks for spoken dialogue system planning yields significant performance gains and paves the way for further research opportunities in the field.

We introduce new semiclassical invariants, and adapt the Euler characteristic formula, for semistable coherent sheaves of a specific class on a complex curve that has an algebraically closed field and complex dimension at least 2. Additionally, we establish connections to fundamental concepts, such as moduli spaces of sheaves, their associated characteristic numbers, line bundles, and their associated geometric invariant theory. These adaptations, in turn, enable the derivation of further information, including transitions in invariants across curves through a specific process, and the identification of further characteristics related to sheaves, such as their dimensions and associated line bundles, and their relationship with the curve's topological properties.

In secret sharing, we aim to establish a random distribution of secrets, such that only groups with a certain entitlement can recover the information, while others cannot gain any advantage. We study the maximum probability that parties who shouldn't have access to the secret can accidentally gain information in the context of the universal access structure, where every group with a entitlement to the secret has access to it. We find a theoretical limit on this probability and construct schemes that achieve this bound in the case of UACS, as well as non-UACS structures. Additionally, we introduce a new constraint that is more stringent than the Shannon constraints but still compatible with existing schemes, and demonstrate that these constraints can be expressed using the properties of a specific type of matrices.

We've developed an innovative approach for precisely measuring entanglement in polarization qubits  networks, surpassing standard methods. By applying our method, optimal precision can be achieved for various  qubit configurations, from two to ten, with substantial improvements in precision. We've also applied this technique to a case of interest: two pairs of entangled photons, showing that our method can reduce measurement errors by as much as 50% compared to using standard techniques. Our approach not only provides accurate results but also yields analytical expressions for standard deviation, enabling efficient processing. We've further demonstrated the method's potential in quantum communication by presenting a protocol for secure key distribution in a dense coding scheme, where highly entangled states can enable positive keys in scenarios  impossible with standard quantum communication methods.

The study of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in plasmas, specifically the properties and occurrences of magnetic reconnection events, is an area of research. Our research focuses on identifying and analyzing the formation, evolution, and disappearance of current sheets within a three-dimensional plasma simulation. Using a simulation with freely developing micro-instabilities, we have analyzed the properties of magnetic islands and sheets in a simulation and found that the simulation accurately reflects real-world plasma behavior. Our results show that the simulation accurately reflects the plasma's behavior through the appearance and disappearance of islands and sheets. Our simulation also reveals a significant reconnection rate and the stabilization of current sheets through the occurrences of kink and tearing modes.

Frozen-pretrained models have been the standard for solving image classification problems. Nonetheless, they struggle with continual learning due to limited flexibility. Our research delves into the causes of this limitation and offers a solution by enhancing it. We achieve this by further constraining the model's output space in line with the cumulative labels from previous tasks. This method significantly reduces interference and operation difficulties, leading to notable performance improvements across three different frozen-pretrained models for two benchmark tests. Our findings suggest that the enhancement's success largely depends on maintaining the model's function as a frozen entity.

As social media platforms grow, so does the issue of hate speech online, which can lead to severe consequences such as mental illness and violent attacks. Effective moderation of hate speech is thus essential. While current methods of automatic detection through NLP techniques have made progress, they still struggle to handle the nuanced, often implicit nature of hate speech expressed in languages like Arabic. This research introduces a new, two-stage deep learning approach for identifying hate speech in Arabic text. Building upon a large, multilingual dataset, the study develops an initial classifier to distinguish between offensive and non-offensive content, and then introduces a graph-based algorithm to split offensive data into supportive and anti-supportive categories. When evaluated on a gold-standard dataset, the proposed model achieved a remarkable 93% accuracy in classifying online comments.

We explore the behavior of large networks of theta neurons, in which the inclusion of an existing neuron's connection increases the likelihood of its incoming connections. This setup facilitates a more nuanced examination of activity patterns in random networks, with varying degree distributions and the potential for zero-inflated models. By applying a mean-field approach, we successfully analyze and predict the conditions under which different levels of neuronal activation emerge. Our analysis reveals that introducing diversity in neuronal connections via degree distribution can dampen oscillations in inhibitory networks and reduce the probability of synchronous firing. This also enables the transition from sparse to dense networks, where most neurons receive multiple connections, without triggering excessive neuronal activation. Furthermore, the use of degree sequences allows us to examine and predict the behavior of degree-dependent networks. Our research demonstrates that activity patterns in these networks can be accurately predicted by a simplified approach that accounts for degree sequences alone.

Recent years have seen the application of various neural network-based methods in program repair. This research focuses on two key aspects of neural repair. Firstly, it examines how Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can be utilized to create a compiler that produces bug-free code, leveraging the knowledge gained from a database of successful compilation results, even without explicit access to the source code, reminiscent of the GAN approach. Secondly, it explores the use of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in the repair process, yielding two key findings. Our experiments indicate that both GAN and RL-based methods can yield positive results in specific, limited scenarios, but do not yield robust general solutions, underscoring the potential of using these techniques as supplementary tools, rather than primary program repair methods.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a non-symmetric interference channel, applicable to a broad range of channel models. Building on a coding scheme that combines decoding strategies, the proposed scheme enables receivers to separately decode messages from both users. Focusing on a specific type of coding with the power of memory, a characterization is achieved, implying that there exists another coding scheme whose memory requirement approaches zero as its performance converges to that of an ideal scheme. The results are particularly significant for finite channel models, implying that optimal performance can be attained with a negligible memory requirement. As a demonstration of the framework's effectiveness, a complete capacity characterization is derived for the discrete interference channel with real output.

We're investigating the Equation-of-State (EoS) and its effect on the dynamics of nuclear collisions, specifically focusing on how it impacts the expansion of quark-gluon plasma and hadrons. We've employed the relativistic viscous hydrodynamics framework and the ideal hydrodynamics model to study this, using data from RHIC and LHC to calibrate our models. We've found that both models are capable of explaining various experimental measurements, including $v_2$ and $v_3$ of different particles, but our research indicates that EoS has a significant effect on the nuclear EoS, as demonstrated by our analysis of the equation of state. We've found that an inelastic coefficient of shear viscosity of 0.08 is sufficient to explain various experimental measurements, as opposed to an inelastic coefficient of shear viscosity of 0.12 for an inelastic coefficient of shear viscosity of 0.08. Furthermore, our research indicates that an inelastic coefficient of shear viscosity of 0.08 agrees well with perturbative QCD calculations, as demonstrated by our analysis of the equation of state.

The rapid spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has caused a surge in global mortality
rates, with healthcare systems facing immense pressure to manage the overwhelming
number of cases.  To combat this challenge, early identification and accurate
diagnosis of the disease are crucial for effective treatment and containment.  To
address this issue, researchers developed a deep learning-based COVID detector
that utilizes chest X-ray images for accurate diagnosis.  This model leverages
ResNet50, a deep convolutional neural network, pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset.
To enhance performance on chest X-ray images, the researchers applied data
augmentation techniques, including rotation and scaling.  This COVID detector
achieved impressive results with high accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
This success demonstrates the potential of deep learning techniques in effective
disease management and highlighting their significance in addressing the COVID-19
crisis.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an advanced neural network architecture designed to process graph-based data. Recently, GNNs have been applied to various stages of wireless communication systems, including physical layer and higher layer protocols. However, the GNNs used in wireless communications face several challenges, such as dealing with large-scale graphs and dynamic network conditions. To address these challenges, this paper reviews the recent advancements in GNN applications for wireless communications, highlighting research opportunities and future directions.

The most prevalent cause of death in Brazil is the homicide, with the highest mortality rate observed in the youth male population. Notably, the southern region of the country exhibits both the lowest overall and youth-specific homicide rates. This study aimed to provide a detailed demographic breakdown of homicide mortality in 2017, comparing regions and analyzing the characteristics of the deceased. Data on all homicide victims from Brazil's national database was used to provide an accurate account. Our findings reveal that the southern area, characterized by lower homicide rates, is home to cities with significantly above-average life expectancy for young males. Furthermore, the southern region's homicide rates are positively correlated with the gender and age of the deceased, specifically showing a higher prevalence among young males.

We investigate the convergence properties of stochastic gradient descent with decreasing step sizes in smooth, strongly-convex function optimization. We demonstrate that using geometrically decreasing step sizes leads to a geometric convergence rate in expectation, and similarly, an almost sure linear convergence rate can be achieved through an appropriate randomized sampling method. Furthermore, we show that this stochastic variant with decreasing step sizes also yields fast convergence for convex functions, achieving an $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ rate in expectation without requiring coercivity.

AXIAX, a proposed model, addresses the strong-CP issue through an axial symmetry. In AXIAX, gauge interactions break axial symmetry but preserve a subgroup, which is also a gauge symmetry. In a specific scenario where axial symmetry is broken by the Weinberg gluon background, the subgroup remains unbroken. Moreover, the model is compatible with string theory's big-bang cosmology. In string theory frameworks, the Weinberg gluon background corresponds to a three-sphere within a D-brane's near-horizon geometry. In addition, AXIAX can be applicable to flavor problems as well. In a particular flavor scenario, the model is compatible with an $A_4$ symmetry.

The quantum version of the "boxworld" theory is examined to identify the most robust non-quantum features of theory-agnostic post-quantum probabilistic frameworks. In doing so, the concept of memory storage is analyzed, with the most general methods for retaining information about a system's earlier states being defined. It's demonstrated that, in general, the concept of storing memories relies on the system being out of equilibrium. Furthermore, in maximally informative scenarios, the concept of memory storage loses its effectiveness. Post-quantum probabilistic frameworks capable of utilizing the "boxworld" model exhibit distinct characteristics, including significantly higher intrinsic non-quantumness and the ability to encode more complex objects than what is achievable with quantum theory.

We introduce DexGraspNet, a vast dataset comprised of over 1.1 million frames capturing over 16 million poses of objects manipulated by two Dexterous Grippers, enabling us to create a comprehensive simulation of DEX - Disassembly Expert. This involves diverse dexterous grasping tasks, such as grasping and releasing with 3 自由度grippers. DexGraspNet features a rich set of data including 3D depth, RGB images, accurate 3D gripper poses with existential uncertainty ranges, robust detection algorithms and efficient 3D sampling techniques. Notably, it boasts an extensive coverage of COV (Coarse-Of-Variance) space with over 16 million poses spanning 1000+ COV regions. A notable achievement is the seamless transfer learning from data-driven approaches to simulation, where our trained policy outperforms random policies by over 20% success rates in novel tasks.

A novel approach has been created to create individual, compact 3D models of human lungs from a single coronal MRI scan. The system utilizes motion-blurred images to accurately capture lung movement during breathing cycles. A custom deep learning network, named DiML, is proposed to generate a lung image at any specified respiratory phase. Additionally, a training method is developed to generate a predictive model of lung motion. A separate method is introduced to convert respiratory phase information into a regression curve representing inhaling and out-holding phases. Experimental results demonstrate that DiML outperforms competing models in terms of accuracy, and further testing shows the approach's reliability and generalizability. Moreover, a 3D model visualization tool has been developed to illustrate lung motion patterns. This tool's potential to enhance the understanding of lung motion patterns during breathing exercises has been validated. Lastly, a regression model is created to accurately predict lung motion during CT scans based on magnetic resonance imaging data.

We introduce a novel on-device knowledge distillation approach that compresses models without relying on external teachers. By utilizing the limited pool of incorrect labels from incorrect model predictions, we can create synthetic training data within a geometric framework known as hypersimplices. This synthetic information is then combined with rough roughness priors to derive a more accurate and detailed model without the need for extensive annotations. By taking advantage of modern neural architectures, we can effectively perform on-device knowledge distillation. Our method, known as HSISD, is demonstrated on a Raspberry Pi 4 and showcases superior performance to existing on-device distillation techniques.

Two submersion functions with all their level sets being compact are defined as
topologically equivalent if their regular foliations are equivalent under the topology.
We show that this equivalence relation is an equivalence relation and establish a
connection to the Eilenberg Macpherson theorem by proving that it is equivalent to
foliated equivalence. Furthermore, we establish an extension of the Lebesgue,
Vopien and Vopien theorem within this context. For specific functions such as those
with real coefficients, we demonstrate an algorithm to determine whether two such
functions are topologically equivalent.

Ecosystems with sparse vegetation, characterized by scattered plant distribution, are commonly seen in overgrazed environments. To gain a deeper understanding of the underlying causes, researchers investigated the relationship between grazing intensity and plant spatial arrangement. An experimental study was conducted in the Patagonian steppe to analyze how different species of vegetation, including the grass Stipaichnophila and the grass-stem Chionoglobrilosa, respond to varying levels of grazing. An advanced statistical technique was employed to analyze the connection between grazing intensity and plant spacing. The results revealed that reduced plant spacing correlates with higher levels of grazing. An increase in plant spacing was also observed in response to a process called self-organization. Furthermore, the study found that the combination of lower grazing levels, lower plant density, and high species diversity promotes ecosystem stability.

A new "CountSketch" algorithm has been proposed for efficiently computing the top k largest singular values of a data matrix. This approach allows for a significant speedup in processing large data sets by representing the data matrix with a compact sketch. By estimating the singular value spectrum of a data matrix, the algorithm can provide an approximation. This approach has been further improved for distributed data sets by creating a two-stage process. This improved method has been tested on a variety of data sets and has been shown to provide faster computation times while maintaining a reasonable level of accuracy.

A python-based program, aux-field QMC, has been created for computing quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo method and is designed to handle electronic structure problems. The program demonstrates superior speed compared to state-of-the-art QMC codes, with its performance nearly rivaling that of auxiliary code ALFMQMC on CPU and showing significant gains on GPU architecture. In addition to its efficiency, aux-field QMC offers enhanced flexibility, allowing users to easily examine auxiliary field method aspects and user code development.

High-frequency trading, a rapidly evolving field, employs powerful computing systems to execute complex financial strategies. To gain a strategic understanding of its intricacies, researchers can utilize the principles of game theory. In this context, high-level high-frequency trading scenarios can be viewed as extensive games characterized by hidden information. Furthermore, from the perspective of financial stability, it is proposed that effective HFT practices tend to converge towards a specific game outcome known as Nash equilibrium, characterized by optimality based on the concept of Pareto. Utilizing the provided trading data, researchers can analyze and confirm its alignment with theoretical expectations.

We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to $n$ buyers. Each buyer has a private valuation for each item, independent of others, and we test the mechanism's truthfulness. We focus on two scenarios where items have the same value to buyers and distinct values, respectively. In the first case, we find the expected total value achieved by the second-price auction when using the highest reported value as a reserve, assuming items are drawn from a lognormal distribution. We then compare this to other mechanisms like uniform distribution outcomes and a modified version of the second-price auction. We also prove the efficiency of the second-price auction under lognormal distribution and establish upper limits on its performance in other cases.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've introduced an efficient planning mechanism through incorporating external knowledge in the form of entity chains, which allow for more specific information in summary outputs. A novel algorithm has been developed to automatically generate these entity chains by analyzing newspaper articles, and we've integrated this chain-based planning method into the abstractive summarization process within the abstract-abstractive framework. The approach was tested on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, where it yielded better results compared to state-of-the-art models by incorporating automatic-generated entity chains.

The differentiability of a function with n variables can be determined by sufficient conditions derived from the differentiability of single-variable functions. This method has the added advantage of handling cases where individual variables are not continuously differentiable. The developed approach is demonstrated with the example of differentiating a function with multiple real parameters in the context of the Knuth probability E(m,n).

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, enabling the estimation of distinct cognitive-behavioral traits. Existing methods to detect this synchronization in conversations face limitations due to their reliance on specific contexts or conversation lengths. A more versatile approach should be capable of adapting to various contexts and capturing synchronization patterns across different conversation lengths without the need for extensive retraining. Building on previous research, we developed a model to compute similarity between a speaker's voice characteristics in a conversation and proposed using this similarity as a metric for synchronization. This approach was tested in a challenging setting with over 100 hours of conversations from the ASPIRE project, and the results showed that speech signals contain significant information about underlying cognitive behaviors. Furthermore, the proposed approach was found to be adaptable and effective in these conversations.

A recent study on equational reasoning in quantum lambda calculus has led to a significant outcome. This outcome builds on an adaptation of realizability techniques, and as a consequence, it proves the completeness of all potential equivalences available in the calculus.

Calculations of the quasiparticle excitation energies were carried out in both the Laughlin and composite fermions theories, focusing on systems with a small number of electrons. By calculating the energy cost of a point charge in the bulk, both theories yielded the same excitation energy when using the same set of parameters. Similarly, by comparing the excitation energies obtained from each theory, it was found that for $n=1$, the results matched, but discrepancies emerged for $n=2,3,4$. Furthermore, by plotting the quasiparticle energies for various $n$, it was found that the composite fermions and Laughlin theories diverged as $n$ increased, indicating that the composite fermions wave function provides only an approximate description of the quasiparticle.

In the context of glaciology, particularly for modeling thin ice shelves with substantial transverse stresses, we consider a non-linear variational inequality involving a non-convex Stokes operator. This inequality is derived from the non-convex energy functional of ice with defects, leading to a differential inequality with a non-convex non-linearity. We model a simplified version of brittle ice with linear cracks, and through rigorous mathematical analysis, we demonstrate the convergence of this simplified model to a constrained piezometric inequality as a parameter tends towards zero. Our results show that minimizing the convex energy functional of ice satisfies a constrained piezometric inequality, with novel estimates on the critical value of a parameter. This is achieved by novel interpolation techniques, and our model's applicability is illustrated in a simplified scenario.

We examined the star formation rates of 11 starbursting galaxies using a combination of 9CO and 13CO data, focusing on their 2D spatial distribution and outflow characteristics. The relationship between outflow mass, velocity, and star formation rates was analyzed, revealing that outflow mass flux and the ratio of outflow mass flux to star formation rate are strongly correlated. The analysis also showed that our sample's gas outflow properties are comparable to those of other starbursting galaxies when compared to theoretical models. The results indicate a significant mass loss due to outflows, approximately 0.5 dex, which is consistent with the relationships found in other studies of outflows in starbursts. The relationship between outflow kinematics and the properties of the underlying starburst was explored, but the analysis revealed the difficulty in making a clear distinction between the properties of outflows in different regions. The difficulty in quantifying outflow properties is attributed to the complex nature of starbursts and the difficulty in determining the boundaries of outflows. The results suggest that the difficulty in making a clear distinction between the properties of outflows in different regions is a fundamental limitation in the field of extragalactic astronomy.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a microscopic transport model that does not rely on the hydrodynamic approximation. The model was used to generate high-energy heavy ion collisions, and we investigated various aspects of anisotropic flow, including its dependence on centrality, particle type, and individual particle transverse momentum. The simulated results for $v_2$ and $v_3$ exhibited real-life like patterns, including a non-monotonic relationship between $v_3$ and centrality, an increase in anisotropic flow with the use of more massive particles, and a slight decrease in differential $v_2$ as pseudorapidity increased, consistent with observations in real anisotropic medium.

This paper presents a novel robotic swarm system, SWARMS, featuring an advanced communication protocol that ensures swarm coordination without imposing a centralized hierarchy. The SWARMS framework incorporates a transparent mechanism for coordinating robot movements by integrating high-level command parsing with low-level actuation. This allows individual robots to execute synchronized maneuvers independently, even in the presence of hardware malfunctions. Our approach leverages SWARMS' transparent communication and decentralized design to optimize mission efficiency through task load balancing. The system was developed in collaboration with the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, enabling the execution of complex missions such as the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover's photo mosaic mission, and can also facilitate multiple overlapping tasks.

A novel approach to leverage the vast amounts of existing, unlabelled videos for improving the accuracy of a deep neural network trained for a specific task of identifying patterns within video frames has been developed. Existing deep neural networks, which were initially designed for video-based tasks like identifying patterns within video frames, could suffer from a lack of sufficient labelled data or suffer performance degradation due to task-specific adjustments. A unique method was created to effectively utilise unlabelled videos from various sources to improve such networks without requiring labelled data or extensive modifications to the network architecture. A significant improvement of 10% was observed when this approach was applied to video-based frame analysis with just a small amount of labelled data. Furthermore, this approach was successfully applied to a range of real-world scenarios, demonstrating its potential for a variety of tasks.

Bohr's inequality determines the convergence of unit-disc power series within an absolute value and states the limit as 10logbase2, leading to the concept of the Bohr radius, defined by variables' disc size, as and as unit-disc size, as and as unit-disc size. Variations in Bohr's inequality are defined by variables including derivative, integral and other operators. We investigate the $\mathcal{L}$ operator, deriving bounds for the $\mathca{L}$ operator, in comparison to previously established operators, and present results for subordination, starlikeness, and convexity.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau for functional data is investigated. Using a novel functional extension of kernel smoothing, the Kendall's tau can be expressed as a functional U-process. A strong U-theorem is derived for functional data and this U-theorem is utilized to establish the consistency of a functional version of Kendall's tau. A functional data approach for estimating correlation is developed and demonstrated to provide accurate estimates of correlation in functional data.

The Edge Intelligence System is set to play a crucial role in managing the vast data generated by smart cities. In this research, we focus on developing a specific application within Edge Intelligence Systems for Intelligent Transportation Systems. An application called Vehicle Information Management System is designed to collect and process large datasets from vehicles equipped with multiple sensors. VIM application application leverages a distributed edge computing architecture to process data locally with a single point of failure. In order to address this limitation, we propose two alternative solutions to enhance the reliability of VIM applications by integrating VIM applications with the Device-to-Device (D2D) technology. By leveraging VIM applications with the D2D technology, we enhance VIM applications' ability to process data locally through the integration of VIM applications with the D2D technology. We evaluate the performance of VIM applications by considering two key metrics: (i) the average processing speed and (ii) the system's ability to successfully process data. Simulation results show that VIM applications by using both D2D communication and dynamic load balancing outperform VIM applications using both D2D communication and static load balancing in comparison to VIM applications using cloud computing.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for measuring topological features in multi-dimensional spaces and their boundaries, extending upon previous work for two-dimensional spaces. Euler characteristic finds numerous applications across various disciplines, including mathematics and physics. We demonstrate its utility in the context of MRI brain image segmentation, a task that FISH, a deep learning-based segmentation method, often struggles to handle correctly due to miscalculated topological features. FISH's evaluation metrics are impacted by these errors, and our work aims to improve these outcomes by integrating the Euler characteristic. By incorporating a loss term based on the topological Eron feature, FISH's performance is enhanced in terms of its Dice coefficient and the correctness of its total twist number.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model that incorporates a double threshold Allee effect, which effectively captures the risks of population collapse for prey due to predation pressure. By simplifying this model using Stokes' rescaling, we obtain a dimensionless form and employ numerical methods to identify multiple coexistence areas and population extinction due to low prey capacity for predation-limited extinction. These findings align with prior research on single-threshold Allee effects, but our adjusted model reveals significant differences in population dynamics.

The Hirsch Conjecture proposes a relationship between the maximum number of parts of a d-dimensional polytope and its diameter, specifically that the diameter is at most the difference between the maximum number of parts of a d-dimensional hypercube and the number of parts of the polytope. This idea, first presented by Hirsch in 1987, has been disputed by Santos in 2014. In response, the Hirsch-Santos conditions were introduced, which aim to determine which subclasses of polytopes still maintain this relationship. This paper investigates the validity of these conditions in the context of the Knuth Torus, which is a mathematical model of a torus obtained by gluing the edges of a cube together. By showing that certain characteristics of the Hirsch and Knuth examples violate the Hirsch-Santos conditions, we hope to gain a better understanding of the relationship between these conditions and the diameters of certain classes of polytopes.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity the k-torsion in K_i(R) for a positive integer k, focusing on how it relates to the nil-groups G_{n,k}(R) where G_{n,k}(R) equals the intersection of G_n(R) and the centralizer of G_{k-1}, of R-central units in G_n(R).

This paper undertakes a comprehensive comparison of the fully differential cross sections for pp -> ttj, where the top quark decays into a tau lepton and its associated neutrino. The analysis encompasses both off-shell and non-resonant effects, as well as tree-level and one-loop contributions, as detailed in the recent arXiv:2205.00225. Reference to the corresponding arXiv:2205.00224 is made for the simulation framework's description.

The vulnerability of facial recognition systems to targeted attacks poses a significant risk, particularly in high-stakes environments. While existing methods to safeguard against image-based attacks are effective, they require substantial storage for model compression, are susceptible to attack, and demand substantial computational resources for model training. To address these issues, we introduce Facade, a lightweight federated face attack detection system that prioritizes privacy, efficiency, and the training of a general-purpose detector. By incorporating a lightweight one-sided distillation method that preserves privacy and optimizing key operations, Facade achieves high detection accuracy, processing speed, and model size, and can be tested across a range of datasets.

In the realm of autonomous vehicle control, supervised learning has been a prominent approach despite its primary drawback, which is the substantial requirement for a vast amount of high-quality, pre-processed data for testing and validation purposes. To alleviate this limitation, researchers have been exploring techniques to enhance the efficiency of data processing methods, and to incorporate learning techniques for tasks such as prediction and transfer learning in the vehicle control domain. To address these challenges, this study presents the application of reinforcement learning techniques to fill the data gaps and accelerate the data processing workflow in the vehicle control domain for autonomous driving tasks. We showcase the application of reinforcement learning methods to improve the vehicle control system's ability to navigate complex scenarios and situations, and showcase promising results and significant potential for future vehicle control system applications.

Evolutionary algorithms have been applied across diverse fields, but their performance can be sensitive to premature convergence. A potential solution lies in using parallel processing, but it can be impacted by evaluation time bias. A recent study explored how evaluation time bias affects the performance of a parallel algorithm under time constraints. Using 3S-NSGA-II on single- and many-core systems, the research found that the performance distribution of many-core systems was non-deterministic. However, increasing processors and limiting solutions per core were both found to be effective in minimizing evaluation time bias. This finding was applied to compare single- and many-core systems, revealing that many-core systems are more suitable for evaluation time bias mitigation.

The Kepler-1646 star system, a rare example of the most common type of exoplanet, has been discovered orbiting a single star. Located 1300 light years away, this planet has a mass between that of a star and a planet and is situated at a distance where such objects are rare. By analyzing its orbit and mass, the study found that it occupies a unique position at a mass ratio inflection point. This discovery provides valuable insight into the formation of such objects. Its unusual mass and orbit also make it a valuable target for further study using ground and space-based facilities.

The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet generator emerges from the dynamics of a periodically driven quantum system. Our analysis reveals that the Floquet generator actually comprises two distinct phases. One phase is characterized by a generator with a norm of the same order as the driving frequency. In contrast, the second phase is associated with a generator that greatly exceeds the driving frequency. We demonstrate, through a mathematical proof, the existence of two distinct phases of the Floquet generator and provide numerical evidence supporting our claims.

Our examination of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ reveals the presence of long-range antiferromagnetic order at x = 0.4, with the Neel temperature (TN) decreasing in the range 0 < x < 0.6 due to reduced phase space for Pauli paramagnets. Beyond x = 0.6, the material exhibits glassy magnetic behavior, with NMR and NQR experiments revealing a distribution of local relaxation rates. This research aims to clarify the link between the material's electronic and magnetic properties through the analysis of the temperature dependence of the 113Cd NMR line width in the vicinity of cadmium impurities.

Our in-depth examination of a high-mass star-forming region, N11N113, utilized a sensitive 21-cm survey to study the impact of radiation from the central massive cluster on surrounding molecular gas. With a high signal-to-noise ratio and spatial resolution, we detected both hydrogen emission and absorption lines in multiple velocity channels. We discovered numerous hydrogen absorption lines in the spectrum, providing the first clear evidence of self-absorption in this source. We calculated the physical properties of the absorbing gas, including its density and temperature, and found that it has low mass but high velocity dispersion. These properties indicate that the absorption lines originate from the cold, dense, and highly turbulent gas near the central cluster. Furthermore, by comparing the observed data to models, we calculated the area of the absorption lines and estimated the mass of the absorption lines to be approximately 0.001 solar masses.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a corresponding greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a zero hole, establishing their measure-isomorphism as well. This comes from the observation that the effects of such an intermediate transformation can be viewed as simulating the associated greedy beta-transformation with a zero hole, while its zero image contains the interval $[0,1]$. We derive measure bounds for the new transformation based on those for the associated greedy transformation with a zero hole. We show that measure-theoretic results previously obtained for greedy alpha-beta mappings hold for these intermediate transformations as well. Moreover, we obtain new measure-theoretic outcomes for these transformations, which were previously unknown. We provide measure bounds for the new transformations, while also examining the effects of perturbations in the base of these transformations, as well as their relationship with constant-expanding map translations in measure theory.

The study of 237 candidate events, representing the rare decay $\bar B^0_s\to D^{*+}\overline{D}^-$, was carried out using 11.2 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the LHCb experiment at a range of centre-of-mass energies. A reconstruction of these candidates occurred in an environment that was heavily influenced by other events. A sophisticated method, known as the Dalitz plot analysis, allowed the measurement of a CP-violating phase $\phi_s$ to be determined. This phase was found to be 0.02 (with statistical error) and 0.01 (with systematic error), aligning perfectly with the predictions of the standard model. Additionally, CP-violating angles $\Phi_M$ and delta $\sigma$ were determined to be 0.94 and 0.01 respectively, with corresponding systematic errors.

It is widely acknowledged that deep neural networks excel at extracting meaningful features from data, but they often falter in generalizing to datasets with different underlying patterns. We've developed a new metric to measure the discrepancy between feature sets, and it's shown to correlate strongly with the generalization performance of deep neural networks. This metric paves the way for effective model feature transformation, which in turn could lead to optimal model training and the most accurate predictions.

In a two-dimensional plane over a finite field with at least five elements, any subset of the plane consisting of at least $q+1$ elements without subgroups of order four is by definition an arc. Arcs of size $q+2$ are either $\mathbb{F}_q$-rational with points forming a conic, or they contain a line that does not intersect any other conic.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it is visually represented by illustrating the triangle corresponding to the subset $\{4, 5, 8, 11\}$ when $n$ is $10$.

Artificial Intelligence applications of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are challenging to interpret, and existing explanations do not meet rigorous standards of mathematical correctness, are computationally expensive, or fail to address actual human queries. To address these issues, we developed a new approach that provides consistent, computable, and efficient post-hoc explanations. Our method, based on SHAP values, utilizes the structure of GNNs to create an efficient approximation that runs in linear time with respect to the number of layers. Our approach is mathematically grounded, and the significant Complementary Component is defined by data, rather than model-specific. Additionally, we validated the high correlation of approximations across multiple GNNs and datasets. Our proposed technique enables responses to various types of explanatory queries within a single framework. Through both synthetic and real-world experiments, we demonstrated the high accuracy of our approach in identifying graph structures and node features that contribute positively to GNN predictions. The code and related materials can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/CoAI-Lab/CGC.

These sources are characterized by the presence of a hot, energetic core and exhibit distinct patterns in their X-ray emissions. The system under study was identified through its position in a three-dimensional catalog and was further investigated using X-ray and radio data. The data revealed that RXCJ0232.2-4420 has a cool core and exhibits certain characteristics, including a high ratio of total pressure to its central value and the presence of radio emissions.
